content: Provider-assisted referral is a client-directed process that occurs within a timeframe that the client feels comfortable with. Once partners are contacted, either by the client or by EDARP staff, they are referred to EDARP facilities for HIV testing services (HTS). Several EDARP clinics now offer early morning and late evening services, specifically targeting men and their partners. Contacts identified through partner services can access testing at these facilities. Common challenges in delivering partner notification services (PNS) include client reluctance to identify sexual partners involved in transactional relationships or those providing non-monetary support, elicited contacts reacting negatively to the information, and hostile responses from contacts. For clients who test negative, post-test services include providing targeted information about prevention services relevant to their needs. Staff support linkage to HIV prevention services through direct client escort, including voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC), prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). Among HIV-negative individuals identified through PNS, 21% are receiving PrEP. The World Health Organization (WHO) maintains a database of complaints for in vitro diagnostics (IVDs) within the scope of WHO prequalification as part of post-market surveillance. IVD manufacturers are required to report serious and moderate complaints to WHO within specific timelines. Additionally, any end-user can report a complaint directly to WHO, which then informs the IVD manufacturer. WHO prequalification primarily focuses on IVDs used in low-resource settings, supporting WHO Member States where preand post-market regulation for IVDs is not well implemented. Since 2015, 113 complaints have been reported to WHO for HIV IVDs, with 32% classified as serious, 49% as moderate, and 19% as mild. For each complaint, WHO requests an investigation report from the IVD manufacturer and oversees the investigation process to ensure timeliness and scientific rigor. WHO works with manufacturers to ensure Member States are adequately informed through field safety notices issued by the manufacturer and posted on WHO’s website. An example of a complaint involved an NGO reporting that testing providers in a national program could not understand sections of the instructions for use of a new HIV rapid test. Upon investigation, it was found that parts of the instructions were in an unfamiliar language due to an editing error by an outsourced translation agency. The agreed corrective action was to issue a new version of the instructions with the correct language and revise the standard operating procedure for translation to include back-translation into English and proofreading by a native speaker of the language. A people-centered approach is essential for a successful HIV response. HIV diagnosis, care, and treatment services should be accessible, affordable, and address the needs of vulnerable groups who often do not seek care. This can be achieved within primary healthcare by integrating services to address the health and psychosocial needs of communities and individuals. Fragmentation of HIV, tuberculosis (TB), sexually transmitted infection (STI), and mental health services can be significantly reduced through people-centered care delivered in a one-stop shop manner at the primary healthcare level, serving as the entry point for HIV diagnosis, initiation, and treatment. The Odessa Test & Treat Clinic employs the AIDS Healthcare Foundation (AHF) approach to integrated testing, treatment, and care, creating a free, comprehensive, patient-centered primary health service as an entry point for service delivery. The clinic provides same-day HIV testing, diagnosis, and linkage to care, using multiplex test kits to increase the appeal of testing services and reach high-risk groups. Partner testing and prevention services for those with partners living with HIV (PLHIV) are included, with counseling offered to discordant couples regarding childbearing. Lay provider testing and peer counseling for men who have sex with men have been piloted, increasing demand for HIV testing during evening and weekend hours. Condoms and information materials on HIV prevention and testing are readily available and distributed to all visitors. The clinic emphasizes rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) within 14 days of diagnosis. ART provision is conducted in collaboration with government institutions, ensuring all services are available in one location. TB screening and prevention are provided according to national guidelines, and reproductive health counseling and services, including cervical cancer screening, are supported by a gynecologist. Modern equipment for gynecological services creates a comfortable and professional environment for women. Clear patient pathways have been introduced to simplify procedures and reduce waiting times for testing, diagnosis, treatment, mental health, and general practitioner services. To reduce stigma, the clinic offers evening appointment hours and Saturday services for HIV testing and ART. The clinic also supports ART linkage through the StART Club, a peer support group that helps individuals with HIV develop and maintain adherence to ART. The club is conducted in an informal atmosphere and facilitated by experts in ART, general care, vaccination, or psychology. Participation helps individuals accept their HIV status, link to care, and connect with a community of peers. Regular communication with medical professionals provides participants with professional and comprehensive health information. The Napneung program in Thailand aimed to improve access to HIV testing and increase the number of at-risk individuals undergoing regular testing. Implemented by the PHPT International Research Collaboration and supported by Expertise France, the program provided free, anonymous, and confidential testing and counseling in four settings in Chiang Mai and Chiang Rai. Outreach relied on distributing vouchers, posters, social media, and Google ads. Clients received preand post-test counseling and rapid testing for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C in less than one-hour sessions. Different counseling methods and reminder strategies were evaluated to encourage retesting among at-risk individuals. HIV-positive clients underwent confirmatory testing and CD4 cell count assessment and were personally referred to partner hospitals for evaluation and treatment. From October 2015 to January 2019, 5733 clients received 7057 tests for each of the four infections, with a median time of 42 minutes between arrival and disclosure of test results. Computer-assisted counseling significantly reduced the time spent by counselors and clients compared to standard face-to-face counseling. Over 99% of clients reported satisfaction with the testing and counseling sessions. Scheduling retest appointments in advance and sending reminders shortly before the appointment was the most effective strategy to encourage at-risk individuals to return for retesting. In Indonesia, a 2017 report revealed that only 35% of TB patients in Jakarta knew their HIV status. HIV testing coverage among TB patients was hindered by the placement of HIV testing services at subdistrict public health clinics, while TB treatment often occurred at primary healthcare centers in sub-subdistricts. In 2018, a joint service delivery technical assistance (TA) strategy was implemented to increase HIV testing coverage among TB clients across five districts. The strategy included mobile HIV testing services, assisted navigation by community-based personnel, specimen transport, and HIV screening using fingerprick tests. Following 12 months of TA, HIV testing coverage for TB patients rose from 47% in 2017 to 93% by November 2018.
